title: Co-ordination of the Pieces
subtitle: Winning back a pawn, and more

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter III, §19 Winning by Indirect Attack, Example 48

steps.title: A pawn is a lot
steps.source: The winning of a Pawn among good players of even strength often means the winning of the game. […] Black is a Pawn behind, and there is no violent direct attack against White's King. Black's pieces, however, are very well placed and free to act.

narration.say: Attacks are not only against the king. Among good players, winning a pawn often means winning the game.
Black is a pawn behind. No direct attack, but his pieces are very well placed and free to act.
Watch how they co-ordinate. First, the rook to the a-file.
White plays a4. His best was b3, but then Black would win the a-pawn anyway.

feedback.*: The knight on c4 takes a piece.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Exchange the knight for the bishop.
exercise.wrong: The knight on c4 takes a piece.

steps.title: Increase the pressure
steps.source: Black could have regained the Pawn by playing B x Kt, but he sees that there is more to be had, and therefore increases the pressure against White's Queen side.

narration.say: Queen to c4. White's rook goes to d1.
Black could win the pawn back now with Bxc3. But there is more to be had.

feedback.*: The rook on e8 goes to the open b-file.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Bring the other rook against the queen side.
exercise.wrong: The rook on e8 goes to the open b-file.
exercise.success: 4...Reb8. Black threatens Rxb2, among other things.

narration.say: Rook to b4, threatening Bd4 and winning the exchange. Queen to g5.
Bishop to d4, check. King to h1.
And the other rook: a8 to b8. This threatens to win the knight.
White must give up the exchange.
Rook to d1, queen back to c4. Black will recover his pawn, with the better game.
